article.title: Actually, sometimes polls underestimate Democrats
article.subtitle: The polling industry doesn't get as much criticism in years like 2025 when surveys overestimate Republicans — but this can be a problem, too.

extraction.summary: Silver Bulletin's mini report card on 2025 off-year election polls, released alongside its updated pollster ratings, which feed the polling averages and forecasts for the 2026 midterms. About 40 qualifying polls of the New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial races and two special House elections had an average error of 7.1 points, against 5.9 points historically since 1998. They also had an average bias of R+6.1, meaning they overestimated Republicans, against a historical D+1.1. The article sets out the pollster-ratings database rules: a 21-day window by median field date, mayoral polls excluded, banned polls excluded, bias computed only for D-vs-R races, and averages weighted by the square root of a pollster's poll count. It argues that pro-Democratic polling bias has mostly been a presidential-year phenomenon, possibly driven by partisan nonresponse among low-propensity Trump voters. It warns that pollsters overcorrecting, for example by weighting on recalled vote, could carry a Republican bias into 2026.
models_discussed: Silver Bulletin generic ballot polling average

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings are updated after each election year, including off-year elections such as 2025, using results from qualifying races. The ratings feed into the Silver Bulletin polling averages and the 2026 midterm forecasts.
findings.rationale: The ratings are an important input to the polling averages and forecasts and are also a public resource.
findings.evidence_quote: they're also an important part of the polling averages and forecasts we'll be using to cover the midterms

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin pollster ratings database includes polls from the final three weeks (21 days) before general elections for president, governor and Congress, going back to 1998. It also includes presidential primary polls, which inflate the database's historical average error.

quantities.name: poll window
quantities.context: final three weeks before the election

findings.evidence_quote: Our database includes polls in the final three weeks before general elections for president, governor, and Congress and goes back to 1998.

findings.statement: The 21-day cutoff for including a poll in the pollster ratings and accuracy analysis is determined by the poll's median field date.

Mayoral race polls, such as the 2025 New York City mayoral race, do not count toward Silver Bulletin pollster ratings. Silver Bulletin keeps this rule even though it lets some pollsters who did poorly in that race off the hook.
findings.rationale: Giving a mulligan to a few pollsters is not a good enough reason to change the methodology.
findings.evidence_quote: But mayoral polls don't factor into our pollster ratings. Admittedly, that gives a mulligan to a few pollsters who had a tough race

findings.statement: Polls from pollsters banned by Silver Bulletin are excluded from the pollster accuracy analysis.
Polling error is defined as the difference between a poll's margin and the actual election margin between the top two candidates.
findings.evidence_quote: meaning the difference between a poll's margin and the actual margin of the election between the top two candidates

findings.statement: Statistical bias, the extent to which polls consistently underestimate Democrats or Republicans, is calculated only for elections where the top two finishers were a Republican and a Democrat. It is therefore not calculated for presidential primaries.

In the report-card error and bias averages, each poll is weighted by the square root of the number of polls that its pollster conducted for that type of election in that cycle, according to the chart notes.
findings.model_version: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings / polling report card

findings.statement: Advanced Plus-Minus measures how a pollster's average error compares to other pollsters' errors in the same election, accounting for which races are harder to poll. Negative scores are better.
findings.rationale: It controls for race difficulty when comparing pollsters.
findings.evidence_quote: how the pollster's average error compares to other pollsters' in the same election, accounting for which races are harder to poll. Negative plus-minus scores indicate that a pollster did better

findings.statement: A pollster's performance in a single cycle should not be given much weight, especially in an off-year cycle where most firms released only one or two qualifying polls.
findings.rationale: Small samples make single-cycle results noisy.
findings.evidence_quote: You shouldn't pay too much attention to how any pollster does in a single cycle, especially an off-year cycle where most firms released one or two qualifying polls.

findings.statement: For report cards, off-year election polls are normally grouped with the following midterm or presidential year; for example, 2025 polls would be grouped with the 2026 midterms.
findings.rationale: Off-year elections are low-key and have few polls.
findings.evidence_quote: which is why we typically group them together with midterm or presidential election years for these report cards

findings.statement: The share of polls that 'called' the race correctly, meaning the poll's leader won, is a poor accuracy measure, especially in uncompetitive races. All 2025 qualifying polls called their race correctly, but none of the races were close.
findings.rationale: Picking the right winner in uncompetitive races isn't impressive.
findings.evidence_quote: Correct calls aren't a great measure of accuracy

findings.statement: Historically, polls showing a 6-10 point margin pick the winner 86% of the time. The rate is 94% for a 10-15 point margin and 97% for a 15-20 point margin.
findings.evidence_quote: Polls that show a race with a 6-10 point margin have 86 percent call accuracy, historically.

findings.statement: Average polling error across all polls in the Silver Bulletin database since 1998 is 5.9 points. This figure is inflated by error-prone presidential primary polls. The 2025 cycle average error was 7.1 points across 40 polls.
findings.evidence_quote: the average error across all polls in our database since 1998 is only 5.9 points — and that figure is inflated by surveys of presidential primaries

findings.statement: In 2025, the 38 gubernatorial polls had an average error of 7.0 points and an average bias of R+6.9. The historical gubernatorial averages are 5.4 points of error and D+0.9 bias.

In the 2025 New Jersey governor's race, 22 polls had an average error of 9.0 points and a bias of R+9.0. The state's historical averages are 3.7 points of error and D+0.7 bias, making 2025 the worst year for New Jersey gubernatorial polls since 2000.
findings.evidence_quote: an average 9-point error compared to only 3.7 points historically, making 2025 the worst year for New Jersey gubernatorial polls since the turn of the century

findings.statement: In the 2025 Virginia governor's race, 16 polls had an average error of 5.9 points and a bias of R+5.8. Since 2001, Virginia gubernatorial polls have averaged 4.4 points of error and D+0.8 bias.
findings.evidence_quote: Since 2001, the average polling error in Virginia gubernatorial elections was 4.4 points, compared to 5.9 points in 2025.

findings.statement: The two qualifying 2025 special House election polls had an average error of 8.4 points and a bias of D+8.4. Historically, House polls average 6.0 points of error and D+1.3 bias. The text says these polls overestimated Democrats, which it attributes mostly to Democrats overperforming expectations in FL-06 and TN-07.
findings.evidence_quote: the two 2025 House polls we added to our database did overestimate Democrats by 8.4 points on average, but that mostly comes down to the blue team overperforming expectations in FL-06 and TN-07

findings.statement: The direction of polling bias has historically been unpredictable from cycle to cycle. The average bias since 1998 is only D+1.1, but 2025 polls had an average R+6.1 bias, meaning they overestimated Republicans.
findings.evidence_quote: Directionally, bias has historically been unpredictable cycle-to-cycle: the average bias since 1998 is just D +1.1.

findings.statement: Average polling bias by cycle: 2016 D+3.0, 2018 R+0.5, 2020 D+4.7, 2022 D+0.8, 2024 D+2.9, 2025 R+6.1. D+ means the polls overestimated Democrats. Pro-Democratic bias has been concentrated in presidential cycles, while midterms have been near-unbiased.
findings.rationale: Possibly partisan nonresponse among low-propensity voters, who turn out in presidential years.
findings.evidence_quote: recently, Democratic polling bias has been mostly confined to presidential cycles

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin considers average bias near zero (such as D+0.8 in 2022 and R+0.5 in 2018) to be about as good as polls can realistically achieve.
findings.evidence_quote: those results are about as good as you realistically can get

findings.statement: Average polling error in 2024 was lower than in any cycle since 1998, yet polls underestimated Trump and Republicans for the third straight presidential election.
findings.evidence_quote: average polling error in 2024 was lower than in any cycle since 1998

findings.statement: Herding appeared less prevalent among 2025 polls than in 2024.
findings.evidence_quote: herding looked to be less prevalent last year than it was in 2024

findings.statement: 2025 rating changes: Trafalgar, which overestimated Republicans by 12.6 points on average in Virginia and New Jersey, fell from B+ to B. AtlasIntel, off by 9.9 points on average, was bumped down to A. Beacon Research/Shaw & Co., which missed New Jersey by 7.4 points, was bumped down to A-.
findings.rationale: Poor 2025 accuracy moved the ratings even with small samples.
findings.evidence_quote: bringing their pollster rating from a B+ down to a B

findings.statement: Best 2025 pollsters by simple average error, with Advanced Plus-Minus in parentheses: State Navigate 2.4 (−4.4, 2 VA polls), YouGov 2.4 (−4.6, 2 polls NJ/VA), Zogby 2.4 (−4.9, 1 NJ), GQR 2.4 (−6.5, 1 NJ), Echelon 3.4 (−2.7, VA), Washington Post/George Mason 3.4 (−2.9, VA). Further down: InsiderAdvantage 5.2 (+0.3), Gravis/Kaplan 5.4 (−1.8), Roanoke 5.4 (−0.2), Clarity 5.4 (−1.0), Concord 5.4 (−4.1, NJ), SoCal Research 6.4 (−0.4), Quinnipiac 6.4 (−1.4, NJ), Research Co. 7.0 (bias R+5.4, −0.3), Beacon/Shaw 7.4 (−0.7). All showed Republican bias. The same miss scores a better Plus-Minus in New Jersey, the harder-to-poll race, than in Virginia.

In 2025 Virginia, according to State Navigate, pollsters who weighted on recalled vote to the 2021 or 2024 electorate (redder years) were less accurate than those who weighted to a modeled, bluer 2025 electorate. Not weighting on recalled vote at all was less accurate than either option.
findings.evidence_quote: pollsters who weighted to a 2021 or 2024 electorate, which were redder years, were less accurate than pollsters who weighted their data to a modeled (bluer) 2025 electorate

findings.statement: There is a risk that pollsters overcompensate after underestimating Trump three times, so the substantial Republican bias seen in 2025 could continue into the 2026 midterms.
findings.rationale: Weighting choices have become a guessing game.
findings.evidence_quote: If pollsters who are worried about underestimating Trump three times end up overcompensating, the substantial Republican bias from 2025 could continue into 2026.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin planned to launch a generic ballot polling average in early 2026 and a 2026 midterm forecast around midyear.
findings.evidence_quote: we're busy preparing our generic ballot polling average (keep an eye out in the near future!) and getting ready to fire up the election forecast (landing date closer to midyear)

political_insights.insight: Polls struggle to reach low-propensity voters, those who vote in presidential races but skip midterms. Trump, and to a lesser extent Republicans generally, increasingly win this group, so presidential-year polls have underestimated Republicans while midterm polls, with high-propensity electorates, have been less biased.
political_insights.evidence: Bias of D+3.0 in 2016, D+4.7 in 2020 and D+2.9 in 2024, versus D+0.8 in 2022 and R+0.5 in 2018.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Do not assume the presidential-year pro-Democratic poll bias carries over to midterms; consider bias priors specific to cycle type.

political_insights.insight: Pollsters disagree about whether the underestimation of Republicans is Trump-specific. Natalie Jackson's hypothesis is that Trump draws out voters who wouldn't turn out in a midterm, and possibly not for a different presidential candidate.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: The direction of polling error may depend on whether Trump is on the ballot.

political_insights.insight: Democrats outperformed polls substantially in the 2025 New Jersey and Virginia governor's races, by about 9 and 6 points respectively. Mikie Sherrill in New Jersey was considerably underestimated.
political_insights.evidence: Bias of R+9.0 in New Jersey and R+5.8 in Virginia.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: This is a possible signal of Democratic strength under a Trump midterm environment, and of pollster overcorrection.

open_questions: Exact direction of the report-card weighting: the chart notes say averages are weighted by the square root of the number of polls a pollster conducted, but it is unclear whether this means each poll gets weight 1/sqrt(n) so prolific pollsters' total weight scales with sqrt(n).
How Advanced Plus-Minus adjusts for race difficulty (functional form, controls).
How Plus-Minus and bias translate into letter grades, and how much one off-year cycle moves a grade.
Whether and how the 2026 forecast or polling averages will account for a possible Republican-leaning bias in 2026 polls.
Apparent inconsistency in footnote 3: the House polls showed D+8.4 bias yet Democrats overperformed in FL-06 and TN-07.
Per-chamber bias values for 2015-2025 in the bias-by-race-type chart are not legible in the rendering.
